title: What is a data race, and what is safe without one

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, thread 1 writes field `a` and thread 2 writes field `b` of one shared object, with no synchronization, and neither thread reads the other's field. What is that?

options.text: A data race, since both writes land in one shared object
options.says: The page says the two fields are different variables, so the writes form no data race.

options.text: No data race, since the writes touch separate variables
options.says: The page answers that there is no data race: they are different variables and the JLS forbids word tearing.

options.text: No data race, since each of the two writes is atomic
options.says: The page defines a data race by unordered accesses to the same variable with a write; its DataRaceExample races on one int although each write is atomic.

questions.stem: Per this page, why can any thread call `SafeSingleton.getInstance()`, which returns a `private static final` field set where it is declared, and always see a fully built object without `volatile`?

options.text: Each thread builds its own copy the first time it asks for one
options.says: The page's SafeSingleton creates one INSTANCE, not one per thread; per-thread copies are what ThreadLocal gives.

options.text: Each call to getInstance() first synchronizes on the whole class
options.says: The page's SafeSingleton.getInstance() is a plain static method that just returns INSTANCE, with no synchronized and no lock.

options.text: Static initialisation runs under a lock the JVM holds for the class
options.says: The page says static initializers run under the class initialization lock (JLS 12.4.2), so such fields are safely published.

concepts: A data race is two accesses to one variable from different threads, at least one a write, not ordered by happens-before.
Static initializers run under the class-initialisation lock, so a static final field is safely published.
